outcome: Since 26 January 2024 nothing has determined the least x with π(x) > li(x) or moved its best known bounds: the best unconditional upper bound is still the Saouter–Trudgian–Demichel bound of about 1.398×10^316 (Math. Comp. 2015), the exact value is still unknown, and the one in-window preprint on this exact quantity (Revers, arXiv 2501.04488, January 2025) refines Lehman's error terms and lists candidate crossings below 10^316 without proving any of them.
problem_asks: Part 1: determine the exact value of Skewes's number, the least natural number x with π(x) > li(x) (π is the prime-counting function, li the logarithmic integral). Some authors use π(x) ≥ li(x) instead; the two differ only when li(x) is an integer, and sources note the difference is minor. Part 2 (implicit in 'smallest'): establish that no smaller x satisfies the inequality, so that the value identified is the least one. Not asked: that sign changes of π(x) − li(x) occur infinitely often (Littlewood 1914); the Skewes bounds 10^(10^(10^34)) and 10^(10^(10^964)), which are upper bounds on the number rather than the number; or any bound on |π(x) − li(x)| that does not locate the first sign change.

events.what_happened: Rosser and Schoenfeld (Illinois J. Math. 6 (1962) 64–94) give the earliest lower bound recorded in the sources: no x ≤ 10^8 satisfies π(x) > li(x). Recorded from Revers (arXiv 2501.04488) references and table, and Wikipedia's Skewes's number article. Neither paper was opened.
events.delivers: Lower bound: the least x exceeds 10^8. Restricted to a computational range; says nothing about where the crossing is.
events.remains: The exact least x; every bound above 10^8.
events.direction: Lower bound on the least crossing; cuts against no statement of the problem.

events.what_happened: Brent (Math. Comp. 29 (1975) 43–56, 'Irregularities in the distribution of primes and twin primes') raises the computational lower bound to 8×10^10. Recorded from Revers's table and reference list; the 1975 paper was not opened.
events.delivers: Lower bound: the least x exceeds 8×10^10. Computational range only.
events.remains: The exact least x; every bound above 8×10^10.
events.direction: Lower bound on the least crossing.

events.what_happened: S. Skewes, 'On the difference π(x) − li(x)', J. London Math. Soc. 8 (1933) 277–283. Assuming the Riemann hypothesis, shows that π(x) − li(x) changes sign at some x below e^(e^(e^79)), which the sources give as roughly 10^(10^(10^34)). This is the bound now called Skewes's first number. Recorded from Wikipedia's Skewes's number article and the reference list of Revers (arXiv 2501.04488); the 1933 paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Under the Riemann hypothesis, a sign change of π(x) − li(x) (so a least x with π(x) > li(x)) lies below e^(e^(e^79)). Conditional on RH. Gives an upper bound on the least x and no location for it.
events.remains: The exact least x; the unconditional case, addressed by the 1955 paper.
events.direction: Upper bound on the least crossing, conditional on RH; cuts towards the existence of a crossing.

events.what_happened: S. Skewes, 'On the difference π(x) − li(x) (II)', Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) 5 (1955) 48–70. Removes the Riemann hypothesis assumption and gives an unconditional upper bound, 10^(10^(10^964)) in the form quoted by Revers and Wikipedia. Sources give the exponent as 959, 963 or 964 depending on how the tower is written. Recorded from the Revers reference list and Wikipedia; the 1955 paper was not opened.
events.delivers: Unconditional upper bound on the least x with π(x) > li(x), of order 10^(10^(10^964)). Gives no location.
events.remains: The exact least x.
events.direction: Upper bound on the least crossing, unconditional; cuts towards existence.

events.what_happened: R. S. Lehman, 'On the difference π(x) − li(x)', Acta Arithmetica 11 (1966) 397–410. Introduces the method of smoothing the explicit formula against a kernel. Revers's table records the result as more than 10^500 consecutive integers with π(x) > li(x) between about 1.53×10^1165 and 1.65×10^1165; Wikipedia's lead and Revers's text give the bound 1.65×10^1165 for the least x. The sources I read state no hypothesis for it. The 1966 paper was not opened.
events.delivers: Upper bound on the least x: a crossing region near 1.53–1.65×10^1165 containing more than 10^500 consecutive integers with π(x) > li(x). The sources I read do not state a hypothesis.
events.remains: The exact least x; everything below 1.65×10^1165.
events.direction: Upper bound on the least crossing; cuts towards existence.

events.what_happened: H. J. J. te Riele, 'On the sign of the difference π(x) − li(x)', Math. Comp. 48 (1987) 323–328. Following Lehman, shows positivity of π(x) − li(x) at more than 10^180 consecutive integers between about 6.62×10^370 and 6.69×10^370, giving the least-x bound 6.69×10^370 (sources also write 6.658×10^370). One search summary says the argument assumes RH for zeros with |γ| < 450,000; Revers's table instead gives a bound 'without the Riemann hypothesis' of about 7×10^370. The AMS record was not opened (403).
events.revisions: The MAA review in the search results dates te Riele's work to 1986; the journal issue is 1987 (vol. 48, no. 177). Hypothesis status is unresolved between sources.
events.delivers: Upper bound on the least x of about 6.69×10^370; the hypothesis status is not settled by the sources I could read (partial RH for low zeros per one summary; unconditional per Revers's table).
events.remains: The exact least x; everything below 6.69×10^370.
events.doubts: The hypothesis status conflicts between sources; I could not open the paper to settle it.
events.direction: Upper bound on the least crossing; cuts towards existence.

events.what_happened: C. Bays and R. H. Hudson, Math. Comp. 69 (2000) 1285–1296. Using the first million complex zeros of ζ(s), show that at least 10^153 consecutive integers near 1.39822×10^316 satisfy π(x) > li(x). This became the standard upper bound for the least x for about fifteen years. The AMS record returned 403 and the paper was not opened. The search tool gave the title as 'A new bound for the smallest x with π(x) > li(x)', but the arXiv paper math/0509312 with that title is by Chao and Plymen; the Bays–Hudson title is therefore unverified.
events.revisions: Journal: Math. Comp. 69 (2000), issue 231. Secondary sources (MathWorld, Chao–Plymen) date the work to 1999; others use 2000. I could not establish which is the first public written argument, so the year given is 1999 with that uncertainty recorded.
events.delivers: Upper bound on the least x: a crossing region near 1.39822×10^316, with more than 10^153 consecutive positive integers there. Conditional on nothing I could find in the sources I read; the zeros used are numerical.
events.remains: The exact least x; everything below 1.39822×10^316.
events.doubts: Chao and Plymen state that the endpoint value of the Bays–Hudson interval was incorrectly stated in the original paper (their Theorem 2) and quote a different figure, 1.401020100×10^316, for the Bays–Hudson bound. Recorded as a discrepancy in the sources, not as a reason to doubt the result.
events.direction: Upper bound on the least crossing; cuts towards existence.
events.object: A region of x near 1.39822×10^316 containing more than 10^153 consecutive integers x with π(x) > li(x), located by numerical evaluation of the explicit formula with the first million zeros. Not an explicit single integer; the existence of a sign change in the region is the claim.

events.what_happened: K. F. Chao and R. Plymen, 'A new bound for the smallest x with π(x) > li(x)', arXiv math/0509312, first posted 14 September 2005; final version (v7, 23 March 2009) states it is to appear in the International Journal of Number Theory (Wikipedia cites IJNT 6(3) (2010) 681–690). Using 2,000,000 Riemann zeros, they show some x in [exp(727.951858), exp(727.952178)] (about [1.39792×10^316, 1.39848×10^316]) has π(x) − li(x) > 3.2×10^151, and at least 10^154 consecutive integers in that interval have π(x) > li(x). The interval is about a factor 12 narrower than Bays–Hudson's (or a factor 10, per other summaries). Their v1 is dated 14 September 2005; I did not verify that v1 already contains the final interval.
events.revisions: v1 14 Sep 2005; v2 7 Oct 2005; v3 30 Nov 2005; v4 23 Feb 2006; v5 31 Jan 2007; v6 8 Sep 2008; v7 23 Mar 2009 ('Final version, to be published in the International Journal of Number Theory'). The date above is v1; whether v1 carries the final interval is unverified.
events.delivers: Upper bound on the least x restricted to the interval [exp(727.951858), exp(727.952178)]; at least 10^154 integers there with π > li. Refines the Bays–Hudson region; gives no exact value.
events.remains: The exact least x; everything below the interval.

checked_by.who: International Journal of Number Theory (refereeing process; published there per the arXiv v7 comment)
checked_by.qualification: A journal of record accepting the paper after refereeing by its editors and referees
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper for publication (arXiv v7 comment says 'to be published'; Wikipedia cites IJNT 6(3) 681–690 (2010)). I did not read the referee reports.

events.direction: Upper bound on the least crossing, restricted to a subinterval; cuts towards existence.
events.object: A set of about 10^154 consecutive integers in the interval [exp(727.951858), exp(727.952178)] at which π(x) − li(x) > 0, located by numerical evaluation of the explicit formula with 2,000,000 zeros of ζ. Not an explicit single integer.

events.what_happened: Y. Saouter and P. Demichel, 'A sharp region where π(x) − li(x) is positive', Math. Comp. 79 (2010) 2395–2405 (HAL 00515378). Per the search summary of the AMS abstract (not opened), gives sharper error terms for Lehman's theorem and a rigorous proof of positivity on a region Demichel had conjectured. Revers's table gives the interval exp(727.95132478) to exp(727.95134682) without RH, with about 6.66×10^152 consecutive positive integers.
events.delivers: Upper bound on the least x restricted to a subinterval near exp(727.951325) to exp(727.951347) (no RH per Revers's table); a count of about 6.66×10^152 positive integers there.
events.remains: The exact least x.

checked_by.qualification: A journal of record accepting the paper after refereeing
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in Math. Comp. 79 (272), 2010. I did not read referee reports.

events.direction: Upper bound on the least crossing restricted to a subinterval; cuts towards existence.
events.object: A subinterval near exp(727.951325)–exp(727.951347) on which π(x) − li(x) > 0 is proved, via a rigorous estimate of Lehman's error terms with numerical inputs. Not an explicit single integer.

events.what_happened: S. Zegowitz, MSc thesis, University of Manchester, 2010, 'On the positive region of π(x) − li(x)' (eprint 1547). Revers's table attributes to it the intervals exp(727.951324783) to exp(727.951346802) without RH and exp(727.951332973) to exp(727.951338612) assuming RH, with about 6.70×10^152 and 1.16×10^152 consecutive integers. The thesis was not opened; the attribution comes from Revers's table, which also says the same source gives a further RH-conditional bound.
events.delivers: Upper bound on the least x restricted to subintervals near exp(727.951325)–exp(727.951347) (unconditional per Revers's table) and near exp(727.951333)–exp(727.951339) (under RH). Counts of consecutive positive integers as given.
events.remains: The exact least x.
events.doubts: The thesis was not opened, so the intervals rest on Revers's table alone.
events.direction: Upper bound on the least crossing restricted to subintervals; cuts towards existence.
events.object: Subintervals near exp(727.9513) on which π(x) − li(x) > 0 is claimed, by numerical computation. Not an explicit single integer.

events.what_happened: D. A. Stoll and P. Demichel, 'The impact of ζ(s) complex zeros on π(x) for x < 10^(10^13)', Math. Comp. 80 (2011) 2381–2394. Per a search summary of the AMS abstract (not opened), this is a heuristic analysis of π(x) using up to 200 billion zeros, and it proposes a bound on |li(x) − π(x)| consistent with Littlewood's growth rate. The summary says it implies Littlewood's constant is K = 1/e and a lower bound on Skewes's number of 3.17×10^114; this is heuristic, not a proof. Revers's table cites Stoll–Demichel for computational evidence of a crossing near 1.397162914×10^316.
events.delivers: Heuristic evidence that the crossing lies near 1.397162914×10^316 and a heuristic lower bound of 3.17×10^114 (per the summary I could read). Not a proof; does not settle the least x.
events.remains: The exact least x; the heuristic is not a bound in the rigorous sense.
events.doubts: The paper's own analysis is heuristic (its approximation to the explicit formula is not the true formula, per Chao–Plymen's summary). Recorded as discounted for bounds rather than as a rejection.
events.direction: Heuristic location of the crossing near 1.3971629×10^316; cuts towards existence, not proved.

events.what_happened: D. Platt and T. Trudgian, 'On the first sign change of θ(x) − x', arXiv 1407.1914, submitted 8 July 2014. The paper concerns the Chebyshev function θ(x) = Σ_{p≤x} log p, not π(x) − li(x): it shows θ(x) < x for 2 < x < 1.39×10^17 and gives an x < exp(727.951332668) with θ(x) > x. Wikipedia's Skewes's number article cites Platt–Trudgian 2014 for a lower bound of 1.39×10^17 on the least x for π(x) > li(x); the paper's abstract does not mention π or li.
events.revisions: Only v1 listed. Published in Math. Comp. 85 (2016) per a search summary, not verified.
events.delivers: Concerns θ(x) − x only. Does not bound the least x with π(x) > li(x). Its 1.39×10^17 figure is about θ, so the Wikipedia attribution to the π problem is a mismatch.
events.remains: All of the bullet, as far as this paper goes.
events.doubts: Not a doubt about the θ result; the issue is that the π-lower-bound attribution in Wikipedia does not match the paper. Recorded as a discrepancy.
events.direction: Concerns a neighbouring function (θ); cuts neither way on π(x) − li(x).

events.what_happened: Y. Saouter, T. Trudgian and P. Demichel, 'A still sharper region where π(x) − li(x) is positive', Math. Comp. 84 (2015) 2433–2446 (HAL hal-01174411). Per the search summaries, modifies Lehman's method (in particular the R5 error term) and establishes a new smaller upper bound on the least x: e^727.951336105 ≤ 1.398×10^316. Wikipedia's lead and a 2024–25 survey in the search results give the same figure. A second form, e^727.951336108 ≤ 1.3971671494×10^316, is attributed to a 2024 paper in a search summary, which I did not confirm. The AMS page and HAL record were not opened (403 and anti-bot page).
events.revisions: HAL record hal-01174411; the Math. Comp. issue is 2015 (vol. 84, no. 295). The HAL posting date was not read.
events.delivers: Unconditional upper bound on the least x: e^727.951336105 ≤ 1.398×10^316 (per the summaries). The restriction set by the method is not stated in what I read; Revers's Section 7 discusses its R5 term.
events.remains: The exact least x; everything below 1.398×10^316.

checked_by.qualification: A journal of record accepting the paper after refereeing
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in Math. Comp. 84 (295), 2015. I did not read referee reports.

events.doubts: The two numerical forms of the bound (1.398×10^316 and 1.3971671494×10^316) conflict in the sources I saw; I could not open the paper to settle which it proves. This is a conflict between secondary sources, not a challenge to the result.
events.direction: Upper bound on the least crossing; cuts towards existence.

events.what_happened: J. Büthe, 'Estimating π(x) and related functions under partial RH assumptions', arXiv 1410.7015 (v1 26 October 2014; v4 25 May 2022), Math. Comp. 85 (301) (2016) 2483–2498. Secondary sources (Wikipedia's lower-bound list, which cites Büthe 2015 at arXiv 1511.02032, and Revers's table) state that π(x) < li(x) for 2 ≤ x ≤ 10^19, so the least x exceeds 10^19. I opened the arXiv abstract page of 1410.7015, which does not show this claim; the claim is not confirmed from the abstract I read. A search summary also gave a 2016 lower bound of 1.2×10^17, which conflicts.
events.revisions: 1410.7015: v1 26 Oct 2014, v2 26 Mar 2015, v3 9 Nov 2015, v4 25 May 2022. The 10^19 claim is cited to 'Büthe 2015' (arXiv 1511.02032, 'An analytic method for bounding ψ(x)'); the date 2015 above follows that citation.
events.delivers: Claimed lower bound: the least x with π(x) > li(x) exceeds 10^19 (per secondary sources). Computational-range type result; says nothing about the location.
events.remains: The exact least x; everything above 10^19.
events.doubts: The 10^19 claim is not confirmed from the abstract I read, and a search summary gives a conflicting 1.2×10^17. Recorded as unconfirmed.
events.direction: Lower bound on the least crossing (claimed); cuts against a small crossing, not against the problem's statement.

events.what_happened: T. Kotnik, 'The prime-counting function and its analytic approximations', Adv. Comput. Math. 29 (2008) 55–70. Computational study that finds π(x) < li(x) for 2 ≤ x ≤ 10^14, giving the lower bound Ξ > 10^14 on the least x (per the 2014 arXiv paper 1409.1780 and Wikipedia). The 2008 paper was not opened.
events.delivers: Lower bound: the least x exceeds 10^14. Computational verification range.
events.remains: The exact least x; everything above 10^14.
events.direction: Lower bound on the least crossing.

events.what_happened: A. Fiori, H. Kadiri and J. Swidinsky, 'Sharper bounds for the error term in the Prime Number Theorem', arXiv 2206.12557 (v1 25 June 2022; v2 17 May 2023). Proves an explicit bound on |π(x) − Li(x)| for all x ≥ 2: |π(x) − Li(x)| ≤ 9.2211 x √(log x) exp(−0.8476 √(log x)), with Li(x) = ∫_2^x dt/log t. The paper is an error bound and says nothing about the sign of π − Li or about the least x with π(x) > li(x).
events.revisions: v1 25 Jun 2022; v2 17 May 2023. No journal reference on the arXiv page.
events.delivers: An explicit bound on |π(x) − Li(x)| for x ≥ 2. Does not locate the first sign change and does not exclude any crossing: a two-sided error bound is compatible with any sign pattern. Remains: all of the bullet.
events.remains: The exact least x; the sign of π − li at every x.
events.direction: Neighbouring result on |π − Li|; cuts neither way on the least crossing.

events.what_happened: J. Elliott, 'Analytic Number Theory and Algebraic Asymptotic Analysis', arXiv 2407.17820 (v1 25 July 2024; v2 31 Jan 2025; v3 20 Apr 2025; v4 21 June 2025). A monograph on logexponential degree. Per the abstract page, it notes that RH is equivalent to a degree statement about π(x) − li(x). It gives no new location, bound or sign-change result for the least x, and it does not mention Skewes's number.
events.revisions: v1 25 Jul 2024; v2 31 Jan 2025; v3 20 Apr 2025; v4 21 Jun 2025 (v4 comment: added abc connections in Section 14.7 and edited the preface).
events.delivers: Nothing on the least crossing. The relevant content is the RH equivalence for π − li, which the bullet does not ask about.
events.remains: All of the bullet.
events.direction: Neighbouring; cuts neither way on the least crossing.

events.what_happened: M. Revers (University of Salzburg, per a search summary), 'New bounds in R.S. Lehman's estimates for the difference π(x) − li(x)', arXiv 2501.04488 (v1 8 January 2025; v2 30 January 2025). Improves Lehman's error terms (including S3), removes the lower condition on η, and reruns the Bays–Hudson, Chao–Plymen and Saouter–Demichel regions. Section 6 tables give narrower estimates of the integral I(ω, η) within existing regions. The paper claims (Theorem 6.1, per the first fetch) more than 4.61877×10^154 consecutive integers near e^727.952018 with π > li. Section 8 gives candidate exponents for a crossing earlier than 10^316 (Table 5). The paper says it is 'very difficult to prove' there are no crossings at those positions and that the graphics 'do not necessarily resolve the real situation'. It claims no new crossing location and no new upper bound on the least x. No journal reference appears on arXiv.
events.revisions: v1 8 Jan 2025; v2 30 Jan 2025 (current; comment 'Improved Theorem 3.1').
events.delivers: Sharper error terms for Lehman's method and narrower numerical estimates within the known regions near 10^316. The count claim (more than 4.6×10^154 consecutive positive integers near e^727.952) refines a count, not the least x. Candidate exponents below 10^316 are discussed but nothing is proved. Does not establish a new least x or a new upper bound on it.
events.remains: The exact least x; whether any candidate in Table 5 is a crossing; the unconditional least-x bound stays at about 1.398×10^316.
events.doubts: The paper's own caveat that its graphics 'do not necessarily resolve the real situation' (Section 8, Remark 8.1). No external doubt found. I found no citing paper or review in the search results.
events.direction: Refines the method and counts within known regions; discusses candidate crossings earlier than 10^316 without proving any. Cuts neither way on the least crossing.
events.object: No new crossing. Table 5 lists candidate exponents ω (for example 316.1456, labelled 'Bays–Hudson region'; 370.8233 'te Riele region'; 1165.2019 'Lehman region') with computed values F_T(ω); only the three known regions are positive.

events.what_happened: T. Tao, blog post 'The integrated explicit analytic number theory network', 15 January 2026. Announces a crowdsourced Lean formalisation project for interrelated explicit analytic number theory results and cites Fiori–Kadiri–Swidinsky's bound |π(x) − Li(x)| ≤ 9.2211 x √(log x) exp(−0.8476 √(log x)) for x ≥ 2. The post permits AI use in formalisation tasks if disclosed and proposes a later stage in which AI tools modify the arguments. A comment reply by Tao says current AI models are '(barely) able to perform this type of adjustment'. No AI system is named. J. D. Cook re-reported the bound on 16 January 2026.
events.delivers: A formalisation project, not a new result. It re-announces an error bound on |π − Li| and says nothing about the sign of π − Li or the least x. Nothing for the bullet.
events.remains: All of the bullet.
events.direction: Neighbouring; cuts neither way on the least crossing.

events.what_happened: A. Bailleul, M. Hayani and T. Untrau, 'A Wasserstein metric approach to generalized Skewes' numbers. I. Prime number races', arXiv 2603.20093 (v1 20 March 2026; v2 24 April 2026). Studies generalized Skewes numbers for prime number races (between quadratic residues and nonresidues), i.e. the first sign change between two comparable prime-counting functions. Per the abstract as summarised, it disproves a conjecture of Fiorilli and gives conditional upper bounds under GRH and an effective linear independence hypothesis. This is a different problem that shares the name; it does not concern π(x) − li(x).
events.delivers: For prime number races, and for generalized Skewes numbers in that setting (unconditional counterexample to a Fiorilli conjecture; conditional upper bounds). Not the classical π(x) − li(x) crossing; does not bound the least x in this bullet's problem.
events.remains: All of the bullet.
events.direction: Different problem sharing the namesake; cuts neither way on the least crossing of π(x) − li(x).

events.what_happened: Anthropic research post, 10 August 2026 (updated 13 August 2026): 'Claude has improved on a longstanding lower bound for the fraction of zeros of the Riemann zeta function that satisfy the Riemann hypothesis'. The post reports that an unreleased research version of Claude raised the proven lower bound on the proportion of nontrivial zeros of ζ(s) on the critical line from 41.6% to 67.2%, and produced a Lean proof (github.com/anthropics/zeta-23-lean). The post does not mention π(x), li(x), Skewes's number or sign changes. This is a neighbouring problem (proportion of zeros on the critical line), not the least x with π(x) > li(x).
events.revisions: Post updated 13 Aug 2026 with a revised paper (per the post as summarised to me).
events.delivers: A lower bound on the proportion of zeros of ζ on the critical line (41.6% to 67.2%). Concerns zeros of ζ, not the least x with π(x) > li(x). Nothing for the bullet.
events.remains: All of the bullet.

systems.name: Claude
systems.what_it_did: Per the post as summarised to me: found the improved lower bound by combining work of Aryan, of Baluyot, Goldston, Suriajaya and Turnage-Butterbaugh, and of Bombieri (2000); produced a Lean formalisation; coordinated subagents that checked 54 arXiv papers and re-proved the result. The claim concerns zeros of ζ, not π(x) − li(x).
systems.basis_quote: it has increased this bound from 41.6% to 67.2%

ai.disclosed_cost: 31 million output tokens over two sessions in Claude Code; about 60 subagents over a day and a half and 2,400 shell commands (per the post as summarised).

disputes.summary: Wikipedia's Skewes's number article gives a 1.39×10^17 lower bound on the least x with π(x) > li(x) citing Platt and Trudgian (2014). That paper (arXiv 1407.1914) concerns θ(x) − x and does not mention π or li. The attribution looks wrong; I have not resolved it for the judging pass.

The Saouter–Trudgian–Demichel bound appears in two forms in the sources: e^727.951336105 ≤ 1.398×10^316 (survey and Wikipedia-style citation) and e^727.951336108 ≤ 1.3971671494×10^316 (attributed in a search summary to a 2024 paper, which I could not confirm, since the Elliott monograph I opened does not mention Skewes). The 1.3971671494 figure may be a different unconditional or conditional bound. Recorded as a conflict.

Bays–Hudson's endpoint is given as 1.39822×10^316 in most sources but Chao and Plymen state the endpoint value of the Bays–Hudson interval was misstated in the original and quote 1.401020100×10^316. Both figures are recorded; which is correct is not settled.

Revers's table attributes the RH-conditional interval exp(727.951332973)–exp(727.951338612) to Zegowitz (2010), while a line in the same table says 'the same source' for a further bound. The attribution is ambiguous in that text.

summary: Nothing in the sources I could reach shows that the least x with π(x) > li(x) has been determined, or that its best bounds have moved since 26 January 2024. The best unconditional upper bound is the Saouter–Trudgian–Demichel bound of about 1.398×10^316 (Math. Comp. 2015), which Wikipedia's lead places as a crossing near e^727.95133 ≈ 1.3972×10^316 (that lead gives no citation). The lowest bound in the record, 1.397166161527×10^316, comes from Christopher Smith's York MSc thesis (deposited 7 March 2017, supervised by Chris Hughes) and holds only under RH, so I treat it as conditional. A 2017 Imperial seminar by Hughes described joint work with Smith and Dave Platt improving the upper bound; I found no paper for that joint work, so I cannot say whether it is the thesis result or a later one. The only in-window preprint on the exact quantity is Michael Revers's arXiv 2501.04488 (January 2025). It improves Lehman's error terms and narrows numerical estimates within the known regions. It also claims a count (more than 4.6×10^154 consecutive positive integers near e^727.952, Theorem 6.1 in the first fetch; the second fetch did not show it) that improves Chao–Plymen's 10^154. Section 8 lists candidate crossings below 10^316 (Table 5), and the paper says these are candidates only. It claims no new crossing point and no new bound on the least x. Within the statement's scope, a count of integers in a region and candidate points are not the quantity the bullet names, so I do not record this as moving the answer, but the count improvement is the closest in-window item and a later pass could read it differently. Other in-window items concern neighbouring objects: Fiori–Kadiri–Swidinsky's explicit bound on |π(x) − Li(x)| (2022), re-announced in Tao's January 2026 Lean formalisation post; Elliott's monograph (2024–25), which uses π − li only in an RH equivalence; Bailleul, Hayani and Untrau's March 2026 work on generalized Skewes numbers for prime races, which shares the name but is a different problem; and Anthropic's August 2026 Riemann-zeta result (proportion of zeros on the critical line, 41.6% to 67.2%), which does not mention π or li. Several of these are AI-related but none is about the least x. AI involvement in this bullet: I found no source that names an AI system involved in the least-crossing problem. Several search phrasings (AI, LLM, GPT, Gemini, AlphaEvolve, Lean) returned nothing relevant, so ai.none_found is true for every event that bears on the crossing. Tao's January 2026 project permits AI use in formalisation and names no system, and it is about explicit error bounds, not the crossing. Coverage gaps and conflicts are listed in disputes and incomplete.
competing_reading: One can read Revers's 2025 count (more than 4.6×10^154 consecutive positive integers near e^727.952, against Chao–Plymen's 10^154) and its Table 5 candidate list as a move in the quantities this area studies, so a later pass could count it as in-window progress. Against that: the bullet names only the least x, and a count of integers in a region is not that quantity, by the same reasoning the abc example uses for scope. Also, the RH-conditional York bound (1.397166×10^316) lowers the best figure, but it is conditional, and it dates from 2017. A reader who counts conditional bounds could say the best known value moved in 2017, which is before the window.
what_would_settle_it: The exact value of the least x (computed with a rigorous sign-change search or proven by an argument that excludes smaller x); a rigorous unconditional sign change located below 1.397×10^316; a published check of Revers's Table 5 candidates; the full text of Revers's Theorem 6.1 and Section 6.4 (the two fetches disagree on whether it is present); the full text of Saouter–Trudgian–Demichel 2015 to confirm which numerical bound it proves and whether it is unconditional; and the Hughes–Platt–Smith joint paper, if it exists.

events.ai_basis: it has increased this bound from 41.6% to 67.2%

judgement.why: The statement asks for the exact least x with π(x) > li(x). All upper and lower bounds on that quantity (Skewes through Saouter–Trudgian–Demichel, the computational lower bounds) predate the snapshot and are bounds; journal publication counts as digestion. Skewes 1933 is RH-conditional but still bounds the same quantity, so I scored it bound. Stoll–Demichel is heuristic, so none. The only in-window paper on the quantity, Revers 2025, sharpens the error terms and the count of positive integers inside regions already known, and lists unproven candidates. It moves neither bound on the least x, so it scores none. That was the close call. Platt–Trudgian (θ), Fiori–Kadiri–Swidinsky (|π−Li|), Bailleul et al. (prime races) and Anthropic's zeta-zeros result address different questions, so I scored them variant. Claude's generated role belongs to that variant event alone and does not carry over to this problem.
judgement.doubts: The Revers count improvement could be read as in-window progress on a related quantity, but the statement names only the least x. The York RH-conditional bound (2017) is mentioned only in the summary and has no event of its own.
